newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: FOCUS-CZECH CENBANK SEEKS BIGGER MARKET WATCHDOG.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-CZECH CENBANK SEEKS BIGGER MARKET WATCHDOG.

text.p: The Czech National Bank (CNB), looking to boost lagging confidence in the financial sector, on Tuesday submitted proposals for parliament to set up a markets watchdog to clean up murky activities throughout the economy.

According to the full CNB report obtained by Reuters on Tuesday, the plan includes creating a "global" organ to oversee regulation on the banking, insurance, and capital markets, including activities of investment funds.
"This (new) institution would, among other things, monitor the activities of diversified financial groups on the markets..." it said.

The CNB's plan appeared aimed at unwinding the Gordian knot of investment funds, banks, and shareholdings which sprung up in the massive privatisation of thousands of Czech firms after the fall of communism in 1989.

The 31-page report, reviewing the forced administration of 12 Czech banks in recent years and the failure of many of them, was prepared ahead of Tuesday's testimony of CNB Governor Josef Tosovsky to parliament.

Tosovsky told the chamber that the failure of several smaller banks must be seen in the context with the transformation of the post-Communist economy and an apparent distaste for regulation of the financial markets.

"There wasn't enough evaluation of the importance of the regulatory framework which must accompany any liberalised economy," Tosovsky told the chamber. "Maybe there was a certain aversion to more regulation."
Tosovsky said the overall banking system -- where more than 70 percent of acitivity is vested in the four largest banks -- was sound, but he honed in on problems in regulation of the capital markets.
Investors have blasted government officials for lax regulation permitting insider trading and murky ownership.
A political battle heated up with the failure of Kreditni Banka a.s. in August and subsequent liquidity crisis at Agrobanka a.s., put under forced administration in September.

The central bank said a crisis of confidence caused by Kreditni's and Agrobanka's connection with the secretive investment group Motoinvest, which made larger banks pull back on the interbank lending market and made Agrobanka illiquid.

The CNB report proposed the new regulatory organ be allowed to "make changes in managment of funds, halt voting rights, and force the eventual sale of shares" held by entities which bring "a threatening influence" to banks and financial institutions.

The CNB called on parliament to mandate more prudence in lending, strengthen the execution of existing regulations, and further enable the prevention of financial crime and "non-concrete" entry of investors into the capital markets.
It also calls for:
- More frequent reports by funds stating the structure of their investments
- Improvement in the capacity of commercial courts to handle cases of bankruptcy and financial crime
- Stronger use of external auditors and harmonisation of Czech accounting laws to match international accounting standards (IAS)

The CNB blamed the problems in recent years of many smaller banks on the difficult trading environment -- especially on the interbank market because of their low volume of deposits -- and the general transformation of the Czech economy from communism.
It said poor regulation mainly of the capital markets -- especially funds in takeover battles with banks -- can weaken the financial strength of banks and lower their credibility.
That responds to allegations by Finance Minister Ivan Kocarnik and Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus who put much of the blame for the banking failures on the Czech National Bank.
Capital market regulation is currently under the auspices of the Finance Ministry.
Kocarnik however told parliament later that he agreed with the analysis of the CNB report, but he did not say if he specifically backed their prescribed remedies.
-- Prague Newsroom, 42-2-2423-0003
